newsitem.title: USA: O.J. Simpson ordered to testify next Friday.
newsitem.headline: O.J. Simpson ordered to testify next Friday.

text.p: The judge in the O.J. Simpson civil case Friday ordered the former football star, who never testified at his murder trial, to take the witness stand at the end of next week, a source involved in the case said.
The ruling by Judge Hiroshi Fujisaki came on the same day he dismissed a woman alternate juror for occasionally dozing off during court sessions.
But jurors will likely have no trouble staying awake next Friday when Simpson begins telling his side of the story for the first time in a court of law.

Legal analysts say Simpson's testimony could be the most crucial chapter of the trial. He is expected to be grilled for several days by the plaintiffs' attorneys, and his performance is all but certain to be a major factor in determining whether he wins or loses the case.

Simpson was acquitted in October of last year of murdering his ex-wife, Nicole Brown Simpson, and her friend, Ronald Goldman. He is now on trial in civil court facing a wrongful-death lawsuit brought by the victims' families.

Simpson's attorneys had tried to persuade Fujisaki to delay his testimony in Santa Monica because he wanted to be present in a courtroom in nearby Orange County where he is fighting the parents of his slain ex-wife for full custody of his two young children.

But Fujisaki spoke to the judge in the child-custody trial Friday afternoon and she had "no problem" with Simpson missing a few days of the Orange County proceedings, which got under way earier this week, the source said.

Fujisaki then sided with the families' attorneys, ordering Simpson to begin testifying next Friday, the source said. Simpson had the right to refuse to testify during his criminal trial, but under the rules of civil procedure he can be forced to take the stand or forfeit his case, which could cost him millions of dollars in damages.

The plaintiffs' attorneys earlier Friday released a list showing they had fewer than 10 more witnesses to call before getting to Simpson. They estimated the others, including limousine driver Allan Park and former Simpson houseguest Kato Kaelin, would be through testifying by next Thursday.

During a court hearing Friday, Daniel Petrocelli, an attorney for the Goldman family, said: "We have a handful of others witnesses (after Simpson). Our side of the case will wrap up not long thereafter."
Simpson's can be called again during the defence portion of the case if his attorneys choose to do so.
Earlier Friday, Fujisaki announced the removal of an 18-year-old juror, who is white, to the remaining panellists, telling them, "Do not speculate as to the reason why."

According to transcripts from a discussion outside the jury's hearing, Simpson lead attorney Robert Baker asked that the woman be removed, saying "I think she has been asleep throughout a large portion of this trial."

The plaintiffs' lawyers objected and alleged that another juror, a black woman, had also been sleeping at times. But Fujisaki decided to dismiss only the white woman for now and said he would "keep an eye" on the other panellist.
During DNA testimony on Thursday, Fujisaki interrupted the defence cross-examination, saying it appeared to be putting one or more of the jurors to sleep. He ordered the panel to pay attention.
The dismissal left six alternates who can be seated on the regular jury if one or more of the 12 panellists are removed.

Gary Sims, a California Department of Justice DNA expert who testified for a second day on Friday, conceded under cross-examination by Simpson attorney Robert Blasier that contamination is possible in DNA testing, but he said there was no evidence that happened in this case.
Simpson's attorneys contend that blood and DNA evidence in the case was mishandled, contaminated and in some cases planted by police investigators.
